programme: IRX3 drives the FTO-IRX3 adipocyte browning/energy-expenditure axis, FOXP2-expressing parabrachial/brainstem neurons supply the central autonomic drive that sets core body temperature, and MYF6 governs the myogenic differentiation programme (CKM, MYOG, MEF2A) that determines thermogenic muscle capacity — together a brain-fat-muscle thermogenesis/energy-expenditure module.
role_in_a: In Metabolic_Rate, this module sets whole-body energy expenditure and thermogenic capacity: IRX3 mediates the FTO obesity-variant effect on adipocyte browning (PMID 24646999, 26287746) and is independently placed in metabolic adaptation (PMID 40743330, 36115924); FOXP2+ parabrachial neurons are experimentally required to sustain core body temperature (PMID 40703448); MYF6 sits in the myogenic gene programme engaged under heat stress and during muscle development (PMID 41418534, 33922304).
role_in_b: No retrieved paper places this thermogenic module as a driver of Stroke. The stroke-linked citations for these same factors describe unrelated downstream phenomena instead: FOXP2 in cortical language circuits damaged by stroke lesions, producing aphasia (PMID 41203433), and a muscle/vitamin-D/sarcopenia paper touching post-stroke muscle status (PMID 36237134) rather than thermogenesis. Post-stroke thermoregulatory and autonomic disturbance (e.g. central fever, hypothalamic/brainstem dysautonomia) is recognized in stroke medicine generally and would implicate the same FOXP2 circuitry, but that link is not present in the retrieved record.
shared_axis: A central-adipose-muscle thermogenesis/energy-expenditure programme built on FOXP2, IRX3 and MYF6 is documented for metabolic rate; brainstem or hypothalamic stroke lesions can damage the same thermoregulatory circuitry, and depressed metabolic rate/energy expenditure is itself both a cardiovascular risk factor for stroke and a driver of post-stroke muscle and adipose remodeling, giving a plausible but unproven route by which the two diseases would recruit overlapping factors.
reasoning: The module is well grounded for Metabolic_Rate by several independent papers on IRX3/FTO, FOXP2 thermoregulatory neurons, and MYF6 myogenesis, and post-stroke thermoregulatory/autonomic and muscle-metabolic disturbance is separately recognized stroke pathophysiology, so the pairing follows from established biology in each disease rather than a documented joint finding. Strength is moderate rather than strong because the actual stroke-side citations for FOXP2 and MYF6 concern different mechanisms (aphasia, sarcopenia/vitamin D outcome) than thermogenesis, so the disease-to-disease link rests on reasoning, and 9 of the 12 concordant factors carry no literature support at all and had to be excluded from the story.
support: PMID 40703448 shows Foxp2-expressing parabrachial neurons are required to sustain core body temperature, and is the one paper retrieved under both diseases (via shared neural-circuitry terms, not a stated stroke role); PMID 24646999 and PMID 26287746 place IRX3 in the FTO obesity-variant circuit governing adipocyte browning; PMID 36115924 and PMID 40743330 place IRX3 in metabolic/hibernation adaptation; PMID 41418534 and PMID 33922304 place MYF6 in myogenic gene expression under metabolic/heat stress; PMID 41203433 links FOXP2 to aphasia after stroke via lesion-symptom mapping, a language rather than thermogenic mechanism; PMID 36237134 links muscle/vitamin D status to sarcopenia in a stroke-adjacent context, not to MYF6-driven thermogenesis directly.
how_to_falsify: In a stroke cohort with brainstem or hypothalamic lesions, test whether disrupted core-temperature regulation (a FOXP2-circuit readout) co-occurs with altered adipose IRX3/browning markers and MYF6-driven muscle thermogenic gene expression more often than in stroke patients without such lesions; if thermoregulatory failure after stroke shows no association with IRX3 or MYF6 pathway activity in fat and muscle, the proposed shared axis is not operating in stroke.
caveats: Both networks were built from blood expression, one step removed from the adipose, brainstem and muscle tissues where this mechanism would actually act. Only 15 patient-group comparisons from 4 independent cohort pairs back the concordance calls. FOXP2 shows 0 of 11 ReMap-confirmed binding events at its listed targets, so direct regulatory action at those genes is unconfirmed. Nine of the twelve concordant factors (TLX2, RAX, CEBPE, ZNF521, LHX9, SFPQ, TEAD2, MIXL1, CDX1) have no supporting literature in either disease and were deliberately left out of the programme rather than forced in. Tissue-generic immune/inflammatory factors (STAT1/3/5A/5B, CEBPB, FOS, JUNB, SMAD3, RELB, SREBF2, FOXO4, NFATC2) were stripped before ranking, so this account should not be read as an inflammatory story; and single-view factors like MYOCD or TBX2, which might tempt a cardiac/muscle-mass narrative, are single-cohort artifacts and were excluded.
